# LAR-001
## Volume I
### Part II - Core Domain

# Chapter 6
# Card Model Specification

---

# 6.1 Purpose

The Card Model represents **knowledge**.

If the Node answers:

> **"What exists?"**

The Card answers:

> **"What do we know about it?"**

Cards contain the descriptive information that gives meaning to a Node.

They are the primary authoring surface for users.

---

# 6.2 Core Philosophy

A Card should contain **one coherent unit of knowledge**.

Instead of creating a single document describing everything about a character, LoreCanvas encourages multiple focused Cards.

Example:

```text
Character Node
│
├── Biography Card
├── Appearance Card
├── Personality Card
├── Inventory Card
├── Goals Card
└── Notes Card
```

This modular approach improves editing, searching, querying, and future extensibility.

---

# 6.3 Responsibilities

The Card Model is responsible for:

- Storing descriptive content.
- Associating content with a single Node.
- Defining the type of knowledge being stored.
- Tracking metadata such as creation and modification times.
- Supporting structured and freeform content.

---

# 6.4 Non-Responsibilities

The Card Model does **not**:

- Define identity.
- Create or delete Nodes.
- Manage Links.
- Execute Queries.
- Control persistence.
- Own Workspace state.

These responsibilities belong to other models or engines.

---

# 6.5 Ownership

Every Card belongs to **exactly one Node**.

A Card cannot exist independently.

The ownership relationship is one-way:

```text
Project
   │
Node
   │
Card
```

The Card references its parent Node through the Node's UUID.

The Node does **not** maintain a list of Cards.

---

# 6.6 Card Identity

Each Card has its own identity, separate from its parent Node.

Required fields:

| Field | Purpose |
|--------|---------|
| Card UUID | Permanent identifier |
| Node UUID | Parent Node reference |
| Card Type | Classification |
| Title | Human-readable title |
| Status | Active, Archived, Deleted |
| Created At | Creation timestamp |
| Modified At | Last modification timestamp |

This allows Cards to be independently tracked while remaining tied to their Node.

---

# 6.7 Card Types

Version 1 provides a flexible system with predefined types.

Examples include:

### Biography

Narrative background of the Node.

### Appearance

Physical description.

### Personality

Traits, motivations, and behaviors.

### History

Chronological events related to the Node.

### Inventory

Items possessed or associated with the Node.

### Statistics

Structured numerical or categorical information.

### Notes

General-purpose observations that do not fit another category.

The architecture should allow additional Card Types to be introduced without changing the core model.

---

# 6.8 Content Model

A Card contains **content**, but the architecture deliberately avoids prescribing a single editing format.

Version 1 should support:

- Plain text.
- Rich text.
- Structured fields where appropriate.

The internal representation of content is an implementation detail, provided it remains compatible with storage, search, and queries.

---

# 6.9 Lifecycle

A Card follows the same general lifecycle as other persistent objects:

```text
Created
   ↓
Validated
   ↓
Active
   ↓
Archived
   ↓
Restored
   ↓
Deleted
```

All lifecycle transitions must occur through the Repository.

---

# 6.10 Constraints

The following rules are mandatory:

- Every Card belongs to exactly one Node.
- A Card must reference a valid Node.
- A Card cannot belong to multiple Nodes.
- A Card cannot exist without a parent Node.
- Deleting a Node must define the fate of its Cards (to be specified in the Repository chapter).

---

# 6.11 Acceptance Criteria

The Card Model is considered correctly implemented when:

- Cards remain modular and focused.
- Every Card is associated with exactly one Node.
- Cards can evolve independently without affecting Node identity.
- The Repository can efficiently retrieve all Cards for a Node.
- The system supports introducing new Card Types without architectural changes.

---

# 6.12 Architectural Notes

The separation between Node and Card is one of the defining characteristics of LoreCanvas.

It enables:

- Modular editing.
- Flexible templates.
- Cleaner queries.
- Easier maintenance.
- Future AI-assisted analysis without altering identity.

This separation should be preserved in all future versions.

---

## Architecture Review

Now that we've completed the **Project**, **Node**, and **Card** models, something important emerges:

```text
Project
   │
Node
   │
Card
```

This forms the **structural backbone** of LoreCanvas.

The next chapter, **Link Model Specification**, won't simply connect Nodes. It will define the **knowledge graph** itself.

In my view, the Link Model is one of the most critical parts of the entire architecture because it transforms isolated information into a connected world. If Nodes and Cards are the nouns of LoreCanvas, **Links are the verbs**. They describe how everything in the fictional universe relates, and they are what make advanced queries and future analysis possible.

So I think the next chapter is where LoreCanvas truly becomes more than a collection of notes and starts behaving like a structured world model.

# LAR-001
## Volume I
### Part II - Core Domain

# Chapter 7
# Link Model Specification

---

# 7.1 Purpose

The Link Model represents **meaningful relationships** between Nodes.

A Link does not merely indicate that two Nodes are connected.

It explains **how** they are connected.

Links transform isolated Nodes into a navigable knowledge graph.

Without Links, LoreCanvas is a collection of independent objects.

With Links, LoreCanvas becomes a world.

---

# 7.2 Core Philosophy

A relationship is knowledge.

It deserves the same architectural importance as a Node or a Card.

Therefore:

- Relationships have identity.
- Relationships have properties.
- Relationships can evolve.
- Relationships can be queried.
- Relationships can contain context.

---

# 7.3 Design Goals

The Link Model is designed to:

- Connect Nodes without merging them.
- Preserve the meaning of relationships.
- Support future expansion.
- Enable advanced Queries.
- Remain lightweight.
- Avoid duplicate relationship definitions.

---

# 7.4 Link Structure

Every Link shall contain:

| Field | Purpose |
|--------|---------|
| Link UUID | Permanent identifier |
| Source Node UUID | Starting Node |
| Target Node UUID | Destination Node |
| Relationship Type | Defines the connection |
| Status | Active, Archived, Deleted |
| Created At | Timestamp |
| Modified At | Timestamp |

These fields define the relationship itself.

Additional information belongs to the Relationship Context.

---

# 7.5 Directionality

Every Link is directional.

Example:

```text
Arin

── rules ──►

Silverkeep
```

The inverse relationship:

```text
Silverkeep

── ruled by ──►

Arin
```

is **not** automatically created.

If both perspectives are needed, they must be represented explicitly or derived by the Repository according to future rules.

This avoids ambiguity while preserving flexibility.

---

# 7.6 Relationship Types

Version 1 defines a set of standard relationship categories.

Examples include:

### Family

- Parent of
- Child of
- Sibling of
- Married to

---

### Residence

- Lives in
- Born in
- Travels to

---

### Leadership

- Rules
- Commands
- Governs
- Serves

---

### Membership

- Member of
- Founder of
- Ally of

---

### Ownership

- Owns
- Carries
- Controls

---

### History

- Participated in
- Caused
- Witnessed

---

### Knowledge

- Knows
- Mentored
- Rival of

The system should support custom relationship types in future versions.

---

# 7.7 Relationship Context

A Link may contain additional contextual information.

Relationship Context is optional but strongly encouraged.

It may include:

- Start Date
- End Date
- Importance
- Confidence
- Description
- Narrative Notes
- Custom Properties

Example:

```text
Arin

rules

Silverkeep

Since Year 842

Until Present

Legitimate Monarch
```

The context enriches the relationship without changing the identity of either Node.

---

# 7.8 Link Ownership

Links belong to the Project.

They are **not owned by either Node**.

Instead, they reference two Nodes.

```text
Project
│
├── Nodes
│
└── Links
       │
       ├── Source Node
       └── Target Node
```

This prevents ownership cycles and simplifies lifecycle management.

---

# 7.9 Lifecycle

```text
Created
   ↓
Validated
   ↓
Active
   ↓
Archived
   ↓
Restored
   ↓
Deleted
```

Link lifecycle follows the same architectural pattern as other persistent objects.

---

# 7.10 Constraints

The following rules are mandatory:

- A Link must reference two valid Nodes.
- Both Nodes must belong to the same Project.
- A Link cannot exist without both Nodes.
- A Link cannot reference deleted Nodes.
- Relationship Type must always be defined.

---

# 7.11 Duplicate Relationships

Version 1 permits multiple Links between the same pair of Nodes **only if** they represent different meanings.

Example:

```text
Arin

rules

Silverkeep
```

and

```text
Arin

born in

Silverkeep
```

are both valid.

However:

```text
Arin

rules

Silverkeep
```

created twice should normally be prevented unless intentionally distinguished by context.

The Repository will enforce this policy.

---

# 7.12 Self-Referential Links

Links where the Source and Target are the same Node are allowed only when the Relationship Type explicitly supports them.

Example:

```text
Organization

merged into itself
```

would be invalid.

But a Concept that references an earlier version of itself might be valid in future versions.

Validation rules determine acceptable cases.

---

# 7.13 Acceptance Criteria

The Link Model is considered correctly implemented when:

- Relationships remain independent of Node identity.
- Links preserve meaning through Relationship Types.
- Context can be attached without modifying Nodes.
- Queries can traverse Links efficiently.
- Duplicate ambiguity is minimized.

---

# 7.14 Why This Matters

Links are what transform LoreCanvas into a knowledge graph.

Instead of storing disconnected notes, the application stores a network of entities and relationships that can be explored, analyzed, and queried.

This is the foundation for advanced features such as timeline exploration, relationship visualization, dependency analysis, and future AI-assisted reasoning.

---

# Architecture Review

While writing this chapter, I noticed something that I think could become **LoreCanvas's signature feature**.

## Relationship Context as a First-Class Model

Right now we've described Relationship Context as "additional information" attached to a Link.

But I think it deserves to be its **own model**, not just a collection of metadata.

Imagine:

```text
Arin

rules

Silverkeep
```

The relationship itself could have:

- its own history,
- attached documents,
- notes,
- timeline,
- evidence,
- source references.

In other words, the **relationship** becomes something users can inspect and expand, not just a line between two Nodes.

That opens up possibilities like:

- Tracking how alliances change over time.
- Recording the history of a rivalry.
- Documenting treaties between kingdoms.
- Showing every event that affected a particular relationship.

I **wouldn't put this into Version 1**, because it would add significant complexity.

However, I think it's important enough to note as a planned evolution. If we preserve the current Link architecture, we can grow Relationship Context into a full model later without breaking existing projects.

That's exactly the kind of architectural foresight I want LAR-001 to capture: keeping Version 1 focused while ensuring today's decisions don't block tomorrow's capabilities.

```
Project

Node

Card

Link

↓

Knowledge Creation

↓

Knowledge Discovery

↓

↓

↓

```

Everything now revolves around **knowledge**.

Not documents.

Not files.

Not pages.

Exactly the philosophy we established earlier:

> **Everything in LoreCanvas is knowledge connected by meaning.**

---

# My recommendation

This is the **last major architectural change** I'd make before we continue.

Instead of:

- Query Engine
- Template Engine

I recommend we adopt:

- **Knowledge Discovery Engine**
- **Knowledge Creation Engine**

The Query system and Template system still exist inside them, but they're treated as capabilities rather than the defining purpose of the engine.

### Why I think this is worth doing

This isn't just a naming change. It better reflects the role these systems play in the architecture and aligns them with the philosophy we've already established. It also leaves room for future capabilities, such as AI-assisted discovery or guided creation, without forcing us to rename or restructure the architecture later.

If we make this change now, I believe the rest of LAR-001 will read more coherently and remain adaptable as LoreCanvas evolves.

# LAR-001
## Volume I
### Part II - Core Domain

# Chapter 8
# Knowledge Discovery Engine

---

# 8.1 Purpose

The Knowledge Discovery Engine enables users to locate, explore, analyze, and understand the knowledge contained within a Project.

Unlike traditional search systems, the Knowledge Discovery Engine operates on the structured knowledge graph created by Projects, Nodes, Cards, and Links.

Its purpose is not merely to find text.

Its purpose is to answer questions.

---

# 8.2 Core Philosophy

Knowledge becomes valuable only when it can be discovered.

The Discovery Engine allows users to navigate their fictional world by meaning rather than by filenames or keywords.

Discovery should feel like asking questions of the world itself.

---

# 8.3 Responsibilities

The Knowledge Discovery Engine is responsible for:

- Executing structured queries.
- Traversing relationships between Nodes.
- Filtering knowledge based on user-defined criteria.
- Sorting and grouping results.
- Providing aggregated information.
- Supporting future exploration methods.

It does not own or modify data.

---

# 8.4 Non-Responsibilities

The Knowledge Discovery Engine must **never**:

- Create Nodes.
- Modify Cards.
- Delete Links.
- Save Projects.
- Manage persistence.
- Change Workspace state.

All modifications belong to the Repository.

---

# 8.5 Discovery Inputs

The engine operates on the Project knowledge graph.

Its primary inputs include:

- Nodes
- Cards
- Links
- Relationship Context
- Templates (where applicable)
- Project metadata

All inputs are treated as read-only.

---

# 8.6 Discovery Methods

Version 1 supports several methods of discovery.

### Structured Queries

Example:

```text id="p34u4i"
Characters

↓

Lives In

↓

Silverkeep
```

---

### Property Filters

Example:

```text id="mq3hmz"
Species = Human

AND

Occupation = Merchant
```

---

### Relationship Traversal

Example:

```text id="8l4lgu"
Arin

↓

Rules

↓

Silverkeep

↓

Contains

↓

Marketplace
```

---

### Combined Discovery

Users may combine multiple conditions.

Example:

```text id="lhddjz"
Characters

↓

Lives In Silverkeep

↓

Age > 40

↓

Member Of

↓

Royal Guard
```

The engine evaluates the conditions without modifying the underlying Project.

---

# 8.7 Query Principles

All queries must be:

- Deterministic.
- Repeatable.
- Read-only.
- Independent of UI state.

Running the same query against the same Project should always produce the same result unless the Project data changes.

---

# 8.8 Discovery Pipeline

Every discovery request follows the same sequence.

```text id="t2jlwm"
User

↓

Workspace

↓

Knowledge Discovery Engine

↓

Repository

↓

Knowledge Graph

↓

Result Set

↓

Workspace

↓

User
```

The Repository remains the gateway to project data, even for read operations.

---

# 8.9 Result Sets

The output of a discovery operation is a **Result Set**.

A Result Set is a temporary collection of references to matching objects.

It does not duplicate project data.

Result Sets may contain:

- Nodes
- Cards
- Links

They should reference existing objects rather than create copies.

---

# 8.10 Performance Goals

The Discovery Engine should remain responsive even as Projects grow.

Version 1 targets smooth interaction with projects containing:

- Thousands of Nodes.
- Tens of thousands of Cards.
- Tens of thousands of Links.

Performance optimizations are implementation details, but the user experience should remain predictable.

---

# 8.11 Extensibility

The architecture is intentionally designed to support additional discovery methods in future versions.

Examples include:

- Timeline exploration.
- Map-based exploration.
- Graph visualization.
- Statistical summaries.
- AI-assisted analysis.

These capabilities extend the engine without changing its fundamental purpose.

---

# 8.12 Constraints

The following rules are mandatory:

- Discovery operations must not modify Project data.
- Discovery must operate only within the active Project.
- Invalid references must be handled gracefully.
- Results must reflect the current Project state.

---

# 8.13 Acceptance Criteria

The Knowledge Discovery Engine is considered correctly implemented when:

- Users can locate information without relying solely on keyword search.
- Relationships can be traversed efficiently.
- Multiple conditions can be combined into meaningful queries.
- The engine remains read-only.
- Future discovery methods can be added without redesigning the engine.

---

# 8.14 Why This Matters

The Knowledge Discovery Engine changes the user's interaction with their world.

Instead of searching through documents, users interact with a structured network of knowledge. This enables richer exploration, more powerful analysis, and a deeper understanding of complex fictional worlds.

---

# Architecture Review

After completing this chapter, I think we've reached another significant milestone.

We now have:

```text
Project
   │
   ├── Node
   ├── Card
   ├── Link
   │
   ├── Knowledge Creation Engine
   └── Knowledge Discovery Engine
```

This represents the **complete knowledge layer** of LoreCanvas.

The next chapter, **Knowledge Creation Engine**, completes the pair. If the Discovery Engine answers *"How do we find and understand knowledge?"*, the Creation Engine answers *"How do we create and structure knowledge?"*

Once both are complete, we'll move into the **Infrastructure** section, where the Repository, Storage, and Workspace bring the entire architecture to life. At that point, every major conceptual piece of LoreCanvas will be defined, and the remaining chapters will focus on how those pieces interact reliably.

## Volume I
### Part II - Core Domain

# Chapter 9
# Knowledge Creation Engine

---

# 9.1 Purpose

The Knowledge Creation Engine provides the mechanisms for creating, structuring, and expanding knowledge within a Project.

It is responsible for transforming user intent into valid Project objects while maintaining architectural consistency.

Unlike the Repository, which validates and coordinates changes, the Knowledge Creation Engine assists users in creating structured knowledge efficiently.

---

# 9.2 Core Philosophy

Knowledge creation should be:

- Structured.
- Predictable.
- Fast.
- Consistent.
- Flexible.

Users should spend their time thinking about their fictional world, not about how to operate the software.

---

# 9.3 Responsibilities

The Knowledge Creation Engine is responsible for:

- Creating new Nodes.
- Creating Cards.
- Applying Templates.
- Assisting with repetitive creation tasks.
- Maintaining consistency during creation.
- Supporting guided creation workflows.

It prepares valid objects before they are committed through the Repository.

---

# 9.4 Non-Responsibilities

The Knowledge Creation Engine must **not**:

- Save Projects.
- Modify persistence.
- Execute Queries.
- Manage Workspace layouts.
- Bypass Repository validation.

All finalized changes are committed through the Repository.

---

# 9.5 Creation Workflow

Every creation operation follows the same lifecycle.

```text
User
   ↓
Knowledge Creation Engine
   ↓
Draft Object
   ↓
Validation Request
   ↓
Repository
   ↓
Project
```

This ensures that no object enters the Project without validation.

---

# 9.6 Templates

Templates define reusable creation structures.

A Template may specify:

- Default Node Type.
- Default Card Types.
- Initial field values.
- Suggested relationships.
- Organizational defaults.

Templates improve consistency while reducing repetitive work.

---

# 9.7 Draft State

Objects being created exist in a temporary **Draft State**.

Draft objects:

- Are editable.
- Are not part of the Project.
- Cannot be queried.
- Cannot participate in Links.
- May be discarded without affecting Project integrity.

Only after Repository approval do they become part of the Project.

---

# 9.8 Batch Creation

The engine supports creating multiple related objects in a single workflow.

Examples include:

- Creating a kingdom with its capital and ruler.
- Creating an organization with several founding members.
- Creating a family tree with multiple characters.

Batch creation improves efficiency while preserving validation rules.

---

# 9.9 Guided Workflows

The engine may present guided creation experiences.

Examples:

- Character creation wizard.
- Location setup wizard.
- Organization setup wizard.
- Timeline event wizard.

These workflows simplify complex creation tasks without changing the underlying data model.

---

# 9.10 Extensibility

The architecture allows future expansion without altering the core engine.

Potential future capabilities include:

- AI-assisted drafting.
- Procedural generation.
- Import from external formats.
- Community template packs.
- Custom creation workflows.

These remain outside the scope of Version 1 but are supported by the architecture.

---

# 9.11 Constraints

The following rules are mandatory:

- Every created object must pass Repository validation.
- Draft objects must never appear in Project queries.
- Templates must not contain executable business logic.
- Creation workflows must not modify existing Project data without explicit user confirmation.

---

# 9.12 Acceptance Criteria

The Knowledge Creation Engine is considered correctly implemented when:

- Users can efficiently create valid Nodes and Cards.
- Templates produce consistent structures.
- Draft objects remain isolated until committed.
- Batch creation preserves Project integrity.
- Future creation methods can be added without redesigning the engine.

---

# 9.13 Why This Matters

The Knowledge Creation Engine is the counterpart to the Knowledge Discovery Engine.

Together they form the two primary ways users interact with LoreCanvas:

- **Creation** turns ideas into structured knowledge.
- **Discovery** turns structured knowledge into understanding.

By separating these concerns, the architecture remains modular while providing a natural workflow for writers.

---

```text
Project

```

Everything above is the **heart of LoreCanvas**.

This isn't just decoration. It gives every future reader a mental map before they dive into the infrastructure chapters.

# Chapter 10
# Workspace Specification

---

## 10.1 Purpose

The Workspace represents the user's active working environment within LoreCanvas.

It is responsible for presenting Project data, managing navigation, and preserving the user's editing session.

The Workspace is **presentation state**, not **Project state**.

---

## 10.2 Core Philosophy

A Workspace should feel like a desk.

Projects contain the knowledge.

The Workspace contains what the user is currently doing with that knowledge.

Closing a desk does not destroy the books on it.

Likewise, closing a Workspace never changes the Project.

---

## 10.3 Responsibilities

The Workspace is responsible for:

- Opening Nodes.
- Opening Cards.
- Managing tabs.
- Managing panels.
- Managing layouts.
- Remembering navigation history.
- Remembering UI preferences.
- Restoring previous sessions.

---

## 10.4 Non-Responsibilities

The Workspace must never:

- Own Project data.
- Save Nodes.
- Modify Cards directly.
- Execute persistence.
- Validate business rules.

Every data modification is delegated to the Repository.

---

## 10.5 Workspace State

Workspace state includes:

- Open tabs.
- Active panel.
- Window layout.
- Selected Node.
- Selected Card.
- Scroll positions.
- Expanded tree sections.
- Current filters.

This information is temporary and independent of Project content.

---

## 10.6 Session Restoration

When reopening a Project, the Workspace may restore:

- Previously opened tabs.
- Active Node.
- Active Card.
- Panel arrangement.
- Navigation history.

This improves continuity without altering the underlying Project.

---

## 10.7 Constraints

The Workspace must always satisfy these rules:

- It must not duplicate Project data.
- It must reference Project objects rather than copy them.
- It must recover gracefully if referenced objects are missing or deleted.
- Workspace corruption must never corrupt Project data.

---

## 10.8 Acceptance Criteria

The Workspace is considered correctly implemented when:

- Users can comfortably navigate large Projects.
- Sessions can be restored reliably.
- Closing the application never damages Project data.
- Presentation state remains separate from domain state.

---

## Why This Matters

The Workspace provides continuity for the user while keeping the Project independent of the interface. This separation allows the UI to evolve without affecting the integrity of stored knowledge.

---

# Chapter 11
# Storage Specification

This is also relatively straightforward.

---

## 11.1 Purpose

The Storage component is responsible for persisting Project data safely to local storage.

It is the only component permitted to communicate directly with the operating system's file system.

---

## 11.2 Responsibilities

- Save Projects.
- Load Projects.
- Create backups.
- Restore backups.
- Export Projects.
- Import Projects.
- Handle schema migrations.
- Manage attachment files.

---

## 11.3 Non-Responsibilities

Storage must never:

- Validate business rules.
- Execute Queries.
- Create Nodes.
- Manage Templates.
- Interpret relationships.

It stores data exactly as instructed by the Repository.

---

## 11.4 Storage Philosophy

Storage should be **boring**.

Users should rarely think about it.

Saving should be reliable, predictable, and recoverable.

---

## 11.5 Constraints

- Every save operation should be atomic where practical.
- Failed saves must not corrupt existing data.
- Backups should remain independent of active Projects.
- Storage should support future schema migrations.

---

## 11.6 Acceptance Criteria

Storage is considered complete when Projects can be safely saved, loaded, backed up, restored, imported, and exported without loss of integrity.

---

# Chapter 12
# Plugin Interface

Even though Version 1 won't support plugins, documenting the interface now prevents future architectural conflicts.

---

## Purpose

The Plugin Interface defines the boundaries through which external extensions may interact with LoreCanvas in future versions.

---

## Design Goals

- Isolation.
- Stability.
- Security.
- Backward compatibility.

---

## Constraints

Plugins must never:

- Bypass the Repository.
- Modify Storage directly.
- Access internal models without public APIs.
- Corrupt Project integrity.

---

## Version 1 Status

Plugin execution is not implemented.

Only the architectural boundaries are defined.

# 12A
## System Quality Attributes

These are non-functional requirements that guide the design of every component.

### Reliability

The application should preserve user data even in the presence of crashes, interrupted saves, or unexpected shutdowns.

Project integrity takes precedence over convenience.

---

### Consistency

At any given moment, the Project should represent a valid knowledge graph.

Partial or contradictory states should be prevented through validation and coordinated transactions.

---

### Performance

Common user actions such as opening Nodes, viewing Cards, or running ordinary discovery operations should remain responsive, even in large Projects.

---

### Scalability

The architecture should support Projects containing thousands of Nodes and tens of thousands of Cards and Links without requiring structural redesign.

---

### Maintainability

Each subsystem should have a clearly defined responsibility, allowing changes to one area with minimal impact on others.

---

### Extensibility

Future capabilities, including AI assistance, synchronization, or additional visualization tools, should integrate through existing architectural boundaries rather than bypassing them.

---

### Recoverability

Data loss should be minimized through backups, atomic operations, and recovery mechanisms.

Whenever practical, failures should be reversible.

---

### Predictability

Users should be able to anticipate the outcome of their actions.

The application should avoid hidden behaviors and implicit changes to Project data.

---

### Offline Independence

All core functionality defined for Version 1 must remain available without an internet connection.

---

### Longevity

Projects should remain usable and maintainable over many years.

The architecture should favor stable data formats and backward compatibility.

---

## Why I think this belongs here

This chapter becomes the **contract** for every future implementation.

For example:

When we later write:

> Repository uses atomic transactions.

The reader already knows **why**:

Because Reliability and Recoverability require it.

# LAR-001
## Volume I
### Part III – Infrastructure

# Chapter 13
# Repository Specification

---

# 13.1 Purpose

The Repository is the **authoritative coordinator** for all modifications to Project data.

It acts as the single gateway between the user-facing systems (Workspace, Knowledge Creation Engine) and the persistent Project.

No component may directly create, modify, archive, or delete Project data without passing through the Repository.

The Repository is the **Single Source of Truth** for all write operations.

---

# 13.2 Core Philosophy

The Repository does **not own** Project data.

Instead, it governs **how Project data changes**.

Think of it as an air traffic controller:

- It doesn't own the aircraft.
- It doesn't own the airport.
- It ensures that everything moves safely, in the correct order, without collisions.

Likewise, the Repository coordinates changes without becoming the owner of Nodes, Cards, Links, or Projects.

---

# 13.3 Responsibilities

The Repository is responsible for:

- Receiving all modification requests.
- Validating requests.
- Coordinating transactions.
- Maintaining consistency.
- Preventing illegal state changes.
- Forwarding valid changes to Storage.
- Returning updated objects to requesting systems.

---

# 13.4 Non-Responsibilities

The Repository must **never**:

- Render user interfaces.
- Store data directly.
- Execute discovery operations.
- Define business content.
- Replace the Storage component.
- Replace the Workspace.

Its role is coordination, not ownership.

---

# 13.5 Repository Workflow

Every modification follows the same pipeline.

```text
User
    │
Workspace / Knowledge Creation
    │
Repository
    │
Validation
    │
Transaction
    │
Project Update
    │
Storage
    │
Success / Failure Response
```

This pipeline is mandatory.

There are no exceptions.

---

# 13.6 Write Operations

Every write request follows these phases:

### Phase 1: Receive

The Repository receives a modification request.

Example:

- Create Node
- Rename Card
- Archive Link

---

### Phase 2: Validate

The Repository verifies:

- Project integrity
- Object existence
- Constraint compliance
- Permission to perform the action (future)
- Transaction validity

---

### Phase 3: Execute

The requested modification is applied to the in-memory Project.

---

### Phase 4: Persist

The Storage component is instructed to save the updated Project.

---

### Phase 5: Confirm

Success is returned to the calling system.

If persistence fails, recovery procedures are initiated according to the Recovery chapter.

---

# 13.7 Read Operations

Read operations are also routed through the Repository.

However:

- They do **not** create transactions.
- They do **not** modify Project state.
- They do **not** trigger persistence.

This provides a consistent access point while keeping reads lightweight.

---

# 13.8 Validation Gateway

The Repository is the only component permitted to approve modifications.

Examples:

✅ Valid:

- Create Character
- Rename Kingdom
- Add Biography Card

❌ Invalid:

- Card without Node
- Link to deleted Node
- Duplicate UUID
- Cross-Project Link

Illegal requests are rejected before Project state changes.

---

# 13.9 Transaction Management

Every modification occurs within a transaction.

A transaction guarantees:

- Either all requested changes succeed.
- Or none of them are applied.

Partial modifications are prohibited.

---

# 13.10 Repository Rules

The following architectural rules are absolute:

1. All writes pass through the Repository.
2. No subsystem may bypass validation.
3. Transactions are atomic.
4. Failed transactions leave the Project unchanged.
5. Repository decisions are deterministic.
6. Storage receives only validated data.

These rules are architectural invariants.

---

# 13.11 Error Handling

When a modification fails:

- The Repository records the reason.
- The transaction is cancelled.
- Project state remains unchanged.
- The caller receives a structured error.

Errors should never leave the Project in an inconsistent state.

---

# 13.12 Dependencies

The Repository coordinates with:

- Project Model
- Node Model
- Card Model
- Link Model
- Knowledge Creation Engine
- Knowledge Discovery Engine (read access)
- Workspace
- Storage

However, none of these components may bypass it for write operations.

---

# 13.13 Acceptance Criteria

The Repository is considered correctly implemented when:

- Every Project modification passes through it.
- Illegal modifications are rejected.
- Transactions remain atomic.
- Project consistency is preserved.
- Storage only receives validated state.
- Components remain decoupled.

---

# 13.14 Why This Matters

The Repository is the enforcement point for every architectural rule defined in LoreCanvas.

By centralizing validation, transactions, and persistence coordination, it ensures that the Project remains internally consistent regardless of how many future features are added.

Without the Repository, every component would need to enforce its own rules, increasing complexity and the risk of inconsistent behavior.

# Chapter 14
# Object Lifecycle Specification

---

## 14.1 Purpose

This chapter defines the lifecycle of all persistent objects within LoreCanvas.

A consistent lifecycle ensures that every object behaves predictably regardless of its type.

Unless otherwise specified, the lifecycle described here applies to:

- Projects
- Nodes
- Cards
- Links
- Templates

Future object types should adopt the same lifecycle wherever practical.

---

## 14.2 Core Philosophy

Objects should never appear or disappear unexpectedly.

Every significant state transition should be explicit, predictable, and recoverable.

The architecture therefore models the complete journey of an object from creation to permanent deletion.

---

## 14.3 Standard Lifecycle

Every persistent object follows this state model:

```text id="0kj2ps"
Draft
   │
   ▼
Validated
   │
   ▼
Registered
   │
   ▼
Active
   │
   ├──────────────┐
   ▼              │
Archived          │
   │              │
   ▼              │
Restored──────────┘
   │
   ▼
Marked for Deletion
   │
   ▼
Permanently Deleted
```

Each transition must be coordinated by the Repository.

---

## 14.4 Draft

Objects first exist as **Drafts**.

Characteristics:

- Editable.
- Not part of the Project.
- No UUID conflicts are permitted.
- Cannot participate in Links.
- Cannot appear in Discovery results.

A Draft is temporary.

If discarded, no Project data changes.

---

## 14.5 Validated

The Repository verifies that the object satisfies architectural rules.

Examples include:

- Required fields exist.
- Parent object exists.
- UUID is unique.
- Object type is valid.
- Constraints are satisfied.

Only validated objects may proceed.

---

## 14.6 Registered

Once validated, the object is registered with the Project.

Registration means:

- It receives its permanent identity.
- It becomes discoverable.
- Other objects may reference it.

At this point, the object officially becomes part of the Project.

---

## 14.7 Active

Active is the normal operating state.

Active objects:

- Can be edited.
- Can participate in Links.
- Appear in Discovery.
- Can be archived.
- Can be referenced by other objects.

Most Project objects remain Active throughout their lifetime.

---

## 14.8 Archived

Archiving removes an object from normal workflows without deleting it.

Archived objects:

- Remain part of the Project.
- Are hidden by default.
- Can still be restored.
- Retain all identifiers and relationships unless otherwise specified.

This allows users to preserve historical knowledge without cluttering active work.

---

## 14.9 Restored

A previously archived object returns to the Active state.

Restoration preserves:

- UUID.
- Relationships.
- Cards.
- Metadata.

Restoration must not create duplicate identities.

---

## 14.10 Marked for Deletion

Deletion occurs in two stages.

The first stage marks an object for deletion.

Characteristics:

- Hidden from normal views.
- Still recoverable.
- Referencing objects may be validated before final removal.
- Allows the system to detect dependency conflicts.

This intermediate state reduces accidental data loss.

---

## 14.11 Permanently Deleted

Permanent deletion removes the object from the Project.

Before deletion, the Repository must ensure:

- Referential integrity is preserved.
- Dependent objects are handled according to policy.
- Storage updates are successful.

Once deleted, recovery is possible only through backups.

---

## 14.12 Lifecycle Constraints

The following rules are mandatory:

- Objects cannot skip validation.
- Active objects cannot become deleted without first entering the marked-for-deletion state.
- Archived objects retain their identity.
- Permanent deletion requires Repository approval.
- Every transition must be recorded in the transaction system.

---

## 14.13 Acceptance Criteria

The lifecycle system is considered correctly implemented when:

- Every persistent object follows the defined lifecycle.
- Illegal transitions are rejected.
- Recovery remains possible until permanent deletion.
- Object identity remains stable throughout its lifetime.

---

# Review

I think this chapter is stronger because it unifies behavior across the entire system. Instead of each model inventing its own lifecycle, they all follow the same state machine.

## One architectural improvement

While writing this, I noticed that LoreCanvas currently defines **states**, but not **events**.

For example:

- **State:** Active
- **Event:** Archive Requested

Those are different concepts.

If we define events explicitly later, the architecture becomes even cleaner because transitions are triggered by well-defined events rather than arbitrary method calls.

For example:

```text id="6s7ixn"
Create Requested
        │
        ▼
Draft
        │
Validate Requested
        ▼
Validated
        │
Register Requested
        ▼
Active
        │
Archive Requested
        ▼
Archived
        │
Restore Requested
        ▼
Active
        │
Delete Requested
        ▼
Marked for Deletion
        │
Confirm Deletion
        ▼
Permanently Deleted
```

I don't think we need to add those event definitions to Volume I right now. They fit better in the **Implementation Guide (Volume III)** because they're about execution rather than architecture.

That means our architecture stays focused on **what states exist**, while the implementation guide explains **what events trigger transitions**. I think that's a clean separation between specification and implementation, and it keeps Volume I from becoming overly procedural.

# LAR-001
## Volume I
### Part IV – System Behavior

# Chapter 15
# Transaction Specification

---

## 15.1 Purpose

The Transaction System guarantees that modifications to a Project are applied safely, consistently, and atomically.

Every change made through the Repository is executed as part of a Transaction.

Transactions ensure that the Project can never enter a partially updated or internally inconsistent state.

---

## 15.2 Core Philosophy

A Project should always exist in a **valid state**.

There should never be a moment where only part of an operation has completed.

Either:

- everything succeeds,

or

- nothing changes.

There is no middle state.

---

## 15.3 Definition

A Transaction is a temporary execution context that groups one or more related modifications into a single atomic operation.

The Repository creates, manages, and completes every Transaction.

---

## 15.4 Transaction Lifecycle

Every Transaction follows the same lifecycle.

```text
Requested
    │
    ▼
Started
    │
    ▼
Validated
    │
    ▼
Executing
    │
 ┌──┴──────────┐
 │             │
 ▼             ▼
Committed   Rolled Back
```

No Transaction may bypass these stages.

---

## 15.5 Transaction Types

Version 1 defines three categories of Transactions.

### Simple Transaction

A single operation.

Examples:

- Rename Node.
- Create Card.
- Archive Link.

---

### Compound Transaction

Multiple related operations executed together.

Examples:

- Create Character.
- Create Biography Card.
- Create Appearance Card.

If any operation fails, all changes are discarded.

---

### Batch Transaction

A large collection of independent operations executed as one logical unit.

Examples:

- Import 500 Characters.
- Generate a city with hundreds of buildings.

Batch Transactions may internally process work in stages, but externally they behave as one Transaction.

---

## 15.6 Atomicity

Transactions are atomic.

This means:

```text
Success

100%
```

or

```text
Failure

0%
```

Intermediate results must never become visible.

---

## 15.7 Isolation

While a Transaction is executing:

- Discovery operations must observe a consistent Project state.
- Incomplete changes must not leak into active Project data.
- Other operations must never observe half-finished modifications.

Version 1 is single-user, but this rule prepares the architecture for future concurrency.

---

## 15.8 Commit

A Transaction is committed only after:

- validation succeeds,
- all operations complete,
- persistence succeeds (or reaches the defined persistence checkpoint).

Once committed, the changes become part of the Project.

---

## 15.9 Rollback

If any stage fails:

- all modifications are discarded,
- Project state returns to its previous valid state,
- callers receive an error,
- the Repository records the failure.

Rollback guarantees consistency.

---

## 15.10 Constraints

The following rules are mandatory:

- Every write operation belongs to exactly one Transaction.
- Transactions cannot overlap on the same modification context in Version 1.
- A committed Transaction cannot be partially reversed.
- Rollback restores the Project to its exact pre-transaction state.

---

## 15.11 Acceptance Criteria

The Transaction System is considered correctly implemented when:

- No partial modifications are observable.
- Failed operations leave the Project unchanged.
- Compound operations behave atomically.
- Repository coordination remains deterministic.

---

# Architecture Review

I noticed something while writing this chapter.

We've treated Transactions as something that exists only during execution.

But from the user's perspective, many creative actions are actually **workflows**, not individual operations.

For example:

**"Create Kingdom"** might involve:

1. Create the Kingdom Node.
2. Create its Overview Card.
3. Create its History Card.
4. Create its Capital Node.
5. Link the Capital to the Kingdom.
6. Create the Ruler Node.
7. Link the Ruler to the Kingdom.

Internally, that's one Compound Transaction.

To the user, it's one action.

That observation suggests a future distinction:

```text
User Workflow

↓

Transaction

↓

Repository

↓

Project
```

A workflow may generate one or more Transactions, but the user doesn't need to think in those terms.

# LAR-001
## Volume I
### Part IV – System Behavior

---

# Chapter 16
# Validation Specification

---

## 16.1 Purpose

The Validation System ensures that every modification preserves the integrity of the Project.

Validation prevents illegal states from ever becoming part of the knowledge graph.

It is the first line of defense against corruption and inconsistent data.

---

## 16.2 Core Philosophy

Validation is **preventive**, not corrective.

LoreCanvas should reject invalid operations before they are committed, rather than attempting to repair damaged data afterward.

---

## 16.3 Validation Levels

Validation occurs in four stages:

```text id="v16a1"
User Input
     │
     ▼
Object Validation
     │
     ▼
Relationship Validation
     │
     ▼
Project Validation
     │
     ▼
Repository Approval
```

Each level builds on the previous one.

---

## 16.4 Object Validation

Checks individual objects.

Examples:

- Required fields present.
- UUID valid.
- Node Type valid.
- Card belongs to a Node.
- Link contains valid endpoints.

---

## 16.5 Relationship Validation

Checks interactions between objects.

Examples:

- Link endpoints exist.
- Cards reference valid Nodes.
- Templates reference supported types.

---

## 16.6 Project Validation

Checks the Project as a whole.

Examples:

- No duplicate UUIDs.
- Referential integrity maintained.
- No orphaned Cards.
- No orphaned Links.

---

## 16.7 Constraints

Validation must:

- Produce deterministic results.
- Never modify Project data.
- Return meaningful error information.
- Execute before Transactions are committed.

---

## 16.8 Acceptance Criteria

Validation is complete when no invalid Project state can be committed through normal application workflows.

---

# Chapter 17
# Persistence Specification

---

## 17.1 Purpose

Persistence defines how Projects are stored, loaded, and migrated across application versions.

It ensures that knowledge survives beyond a single application session.

---

## 17.2 Core Philosophy

Persistence should be:

- Reliable.
- Predictable.
- Backward compatible.
- Independent of user interface concerns.

The storage format is an implementation detail; the architectural guarantees are not.

---

## 17.3 Persistence Rules

Persistence must preserve:

- Identity.
- Relationships.
- Metadata.
- Ordering where required.
- Version information.

No semantic information may be lost during a save/load cycle.

---

## 17.4 Versioning

Every Project contains:

- Project Format Version.
- Architecture Version.
- Creation Version.
- Last Saved Version.

This enables future migration.

---

## 17.5 Migration

When opening an older Project:

1. Detect version.
2. Determine migration path.
3. Execute migration.
4. Validate migrated Project.
5. Open Project.

Migration must never silently discard information.

---

## 17.6 Constraints

- Persistence must preserve UUIDs.
- Save/load operations must be deterministic.
- Migrations must be repeatable.
- Unsupported versions should fail gracefully.

---

## 17.7 Acceptance Criteria

A Project can be saved, closed, reopened, and migrated without loss of meaning or structural integrity.

---

# Chapter 18
# Recovery Specification

---

## 18.1 Purpose

Recovery defines how LoreCanvas responds to failures while minimizing data loss.

---

## 18.2 Core Philosophy

Failure is inevitable.

Data loss should not be.

Recovery is therefore considered a first-class architectural concern.

---

## 18.3 Failure Categories

Version 1 recognizes:

- Application crash.
- Failed save.
- Corrupted Project file.
- Interrupted Transaction.
- Invalid migration.

Each category has a defined recovery path.

---

## 18.4 Recovery Process

```text id="r18a1"
Failure Detected
      │
      ▼
Stop Operation
      │
      ▼
Restore Last Valid State
      │
      ▼
Verify Integrity
      │
      ▼
Notify User
```

Recovery prioritizes consistency over speed.

---

## 18.5 Backups

Recovery may use:

- Automatic backups.
- Manual backups.
- Transaction checkpoints.

Backups are separate from active Project data.

---

## 18.6 Recovery Guarantees

Version 1 guarantees:

- Failed Transactions do not corrupt Projects.
- Interrupted saves leave the previous valid Project intact where practical.
- Recovery procedures do not introduce new inconsistencies.

---

## 18.7 Constraints

Recovery must:

- Preserve valid data.
- Never invent missing data.
- Clearly report unrecoverable failures.
- Keep recovery deterministic.

---

## 18.8 Acceptance Criteria

Recovery is considered complete when every supported failure mode results in either:

- successful restoration, or
- a clearly reported unrecoverable state without further corruption.

---

# ✅ Part IV Complete

This finishes the behavioral contract of LoreCanvas.

At this point, the architecture answers:

- **What exists?** (Part II)
- **How components interact?** (Part III)
- **How the system behaves?** (Part IV)

Examples:

- Every object has a stable identity.
- All writes pass through the Repository.
- Discovery never modifies data.
- Creation always produces valid structures.
- Transactions are atomic.
- Validation precedes persistence.
- Projects remain usable offline.

At this point, I would consider the architecture to be **functionally complete**.

The remaining Part V isn't about the current system. It's about ensuring that today's architecture won't become tomorrow's limitation.

That means Part V should cover things like:

- Compatibility guarantees.
- Extension points.
- Versioning policy.
- Future AI integration boundaries.
- Cloud synchronization boundaries.
- Public API stability.

These chapters won't change how Version 1 works. Instead, they'll define how Version 2, Version 5, or even Version 10 can grow without breaking the foundation we've established.

I think that's a fitting way to end Volume I: not by adding more features, but by defining how LoreCanvas can evolve while preserving the architectural principles we've spent this entire document building.

# LAR-001

### Part V – Future Compatibility

# Chapter 19
# Evolution Principles

---

## 19.1 Purpose

This chapter defines the principles that govern the long-term evolution of LoreCanvas.

Future versions should extend the architecture rather than replace it whenever practical.

---

## 19.2 Core Philosophy

LoreCanvas is designed to grow through **addition**, not **disruption**.

New capabilities should integrate with existing architectural boundaries instead of bypassing them.

---

## 19.3 Evolution Rules

Future development should follow these principles:

- Prefer extension over replacement.
- Preserve Project compatibility whenever possible.
- Maintain stable object identities.
- Reuse existing engines before introducing new ones.
- Keep responsibilities clearly separated.
- Avoid unnecessary coupling between subsystems.

---

## 19.4 Architectural Stability

The following concepts are considered foundational:

- Project
- Node
- Card
- Link
- Repository
- Knowledge Creation Engine
- Knowledge Discovery Engine

These concepts should only change through a major architectural revision.

---

## 19.5 Acceptance Criteria

Evolution is considered successful when new capabilities can be introduced without compromising existing Projects or violating established architectural boundaries.

---

# Chapter 20
# Compatibility Guarantees

---

## 20.1 Purpose

LoreCanvas provides long-term guarantees regarding Project compatibility and architectural stability.

These guarantees represent commitments to users and developers.

---

## 20.2 User Guarantees

LoreCanvas strives to ensure that:

- Existing Projects remain usable after upgrades.
- Object identities remain stable.
- Relationships preserve their meaning.
- Stored knowledge is never intentionally discarded during upgrades.
- Migration is preferred over replacement.

---

## 20.3 Developer Guarantees

Developers should be able to rely upon:

- Stable Repository behavior.
- Stable Core Models.
- Predictable Transactions.
- Consistent Validation rules.
- Documented extension points.

---

## 20.4 Version Policy

Breaking architectural changes require a major version.

Backward-compatible additions should be preferred whenever feasible.

---

# Chapter 21
# Extension Architecture

---

## 21.1 Purpose

This chapter defines how future capabilities integrate with LoreCanvas.

Future systems should connect through existing architectural boundaries instead of introducing parallel architectures.

---

## 21.2 AI Integration

Future AI systems should operate through:

```text id="d4a91v"
Knowledge Creation Engine

or

Knowledge Discovery Engine
```

AI must never bypass the Repository.

---

## 21.3 Cloud Synchronization

Future synchronization should interact through:

```text id="f6e2ak"
Repository

↓

Storage
```

Synchronization should never directly manipulate Project Models.

---

## 21.4 Visualization Systems

Graph views, timeline views, maps, and similar visualizations should consume data through the Knowledge Discovery Engine.

They remain presentation layers rather than new sources of truth.

---

## 21.5 Plugin Expansion

Plugins should extend behavior through documented APIs.

Plugins must not:

- Modify Storage directly.
- Bypass Transactions.
- Circumvent Validation.
- Alter Repository guarantees.

---

## 21.6 Acceptance Criteria

Future systems integrate without violating the responsibilities of existing components.

---

# Chapter 22
# Architectural Boundaries

---

## 22.1 Purpose

Architectural boundaries preserve the separation of responsibilities between subsystems.

Respecting these boundaries minimizes coupling and improves maintainability.

---

## 22.2 Permanent Boundaries

The following relationships are architectural invariants:

- Workspace does not own Project data.
- Storage does not validate business rules.
- Discovery does not modify Projects.
- Creation does not bypass the Repository.
- Repository coordinates but does not own Project Models.

---

## 22.3 Dependency Direction

Dependencies should continue to flow downward through the architecture.

Higher-level systems depend on lower-level systems.

Lower-level systems remain independent of presentation.

---

## 22.4 Acceptance Criteria

Architectural boundaries are considered preserved when subsystem responsibilities remain distinct and modifications occur through approved coordination paths.

---

# Chapter 23
# Closing Principles

---

## 23.1 Vision

LoreCanvas exists to help creators build, organize, and understand complex fictional worlds.

Its purpose is not simply to store information, but to reveal the relationships that give that information meaning.

---

## 23.2 Design Values

LoreCanvas values:

- Clarity over complexity.
- Structure over chaos.
- Consistency over convenience.
- Evolution over replacement.
- Knowledge over documents.

---

## 23.3 Long-Term Direction

Future versions should continue to strengthen the architecture established by this document.

New features should deepen existing concepts rather than fragment the system with competing paradigms.

---

## 23.4 Final Architectural Statement

LoreCanvas is a structured knowledge platform centered on Projects, Nodes, Cards, and Links.

Knowledge is created through structured workflows, discovered through semantic exploration, protected through coordinated transactions, and preserved through reliable persistence.

Every architectural decision should reinforce these principles.

Looking back over this journey, I think the biggest achievement isn't that we've written a long document.

It's that we've **avoided locking ourselves into a brittle design**.

Instead, we've spent the time to establish:

- Stable responsibilities.
- Clear boundaries.
- A consistent domain model.
- Rules for evolution.

# MTDP-001
# Master Technical Design Package

**Project:** LoreCanvas

**Version:** 1.0

**Status:** Approved for Implementation

**Target Audience:** Claude (Implementation AI), Human Developers, Technical Reviewers

---

# Executive Summary

LoreCanvas is an offline-first desktop application for structured worldbuilding and knowledge management.

Unlike traditional note-taking applications, LoreCanvas organizes information into a graph of Projects, Nodes, Cards, and Links, allowing creators to model complex fictional worlds through structured relationships.

The purpose of this document is to bridge the gap between the architectural specification (LAR-001) and the implementation process.

This document defines engineering rules, implementation expectations, coding standards, and execution guidance without replacing the architectural specification.

---

# Document Authority

The documentation hierarchy is:

```text
LCD-000
Documentation Index

↓

LAR-001
Architecture Specification

↓

MTDP-001
Master Technical Design Package

↓

PEP-001
Project Execution Plan

↓

Implementation
```

If two documents conflict:

1. LAR-001 takes precedence.
2. MTDP-001 interprets LAR-001 for implementation.
3. PEP-001 defines execution order.

---

# Project Objectives

The implementation must satisfy the following goals:

### Primary Objectives

- Offline-first operation.
- Structured knowledge management.
- Stable architecture.
- Extensible design.
- Long-term maintainability.

### Secondary Objectives

- High performance.
- Responsive interface.
- Future AI compatibility.
- Plugin support.
- Cloud synchronization readiness.

These objectives guide implementation decisions.

---

# Scope

Version 1 includes:

- Project management.
- Nodes.
- Cards.
- Links.
- Repository.
- Knowledge Creation Engine.
- Knowledge Discovery Engine.
- Workspace.
- Storage.
- Validation.
- Transactions.
- Recovery.
- Local project persistence.

Version 1 explicitly excludes:

- AI assistants.
- Online collaboration.
- Cloud synchronization.
- Real-time multi-user editing.
- Marketplace features.

---

# Engineering Principles

The following principles are mandatory:

### Repository First

All write operations pass through the Repository.

### Single Source of Truth

Project Models own data.

No duplicated ownership.

### Offline First

Internet connectivity must never be required for core functionality.

### Deterministic Behavior

Given identical inputs, identical outputs should result.

### Stable Identity

UUIDs never change.

### Extensibility

Future features integrate through existing architectural boundaries.

---

# Architecture Reference

The following architectural components are defined in LAR-001:

- Project
- Node
- Card
- Link
- Workspace
- Knowledge Creation Engine
- Knowledge Discovery Engine
- Repository
- Storage
- Validation
- Transactions
- Recovery

Implementation must conform to these definitions.

---

# Technical Standards

The implementation should prioritize:

- Readable code.
- Modular packages.
- Clear interfaces.
- Strong typing.
- Comprehensive documentation.
- Unit-testable components.

Complexity should be minimized wherever practical.

---

# Development Workflow

Every feature should follow the same lifecycle:

1. Review relevant LAR-001 sections.
2. Review relevant MTDP guidance.
3. Implement feature.
4. Write tests.
5. Validate against acceptance criteria.
6. Update documentation if required.

---

# Claude Implementation Contract

Claude is responsible for implementing LoreCanvas according to the approved specifications.

Claude must not redesign the architecture.

Claude may improve implementation quality but should preserve architectural intent.

When uncertainty exists:

- Pause implementation.
- Explain the ambiguity.
- Suggest one or more solutions.
- Wait for approval before changing architecture.

Claude should prefer asking for clarification over making irreversible architectural assumptions.

---

# Success Criteria

Implementation is considered successful when:

- Architectural rules remain intact.
- All acceptance criteria are met.
- Tests pass.
- Documentation remains synchronized.
- The application behaves consistently with LAR-001.

- Which architectural shortcuts are forbidden?
- Which coding practices are mandatory?
- How should dependencies be managed?

I think putting those constraints before any technical details is the right move. It establishes the engineering boundaries first, so every later decision about packages, APIs, and data structures happens within a well-defined framework. In practice, that makes Claude's job much easier because it knows not only what to build, but also the limits within which it should build it.

# MTDP-001
# Chapter 2
## Implementation Constraints

---

## 2.1 Purpose

This chapter defines the engineering constraints that govern the implementation of LoreCanvas.

These constraints exist to ensure that implementation remains faithful to the architecture defined in LAR-001.

Implementation quality may improve.

Architecture must remain stable.

---

# 2.2 Architectural Authority

The following documents are authoritative:

1. LCD-000
2. LAR-001
3. MTDP-001
4. PEP-001

Implementation must never contradict higher-level documents.

---

# 2.3 Implementation Philosophy

Implementation should solve engineering problems.

Implementation should **not** redesign architectural decisions.

If implementation reveals weaknesses:

- Stop.
- Report.
- Suggest alternatives.
- Await approval.

Never silently redesign the system.

---

# 2.4 Mandatory Constraints

The following rules are absolute.

## Repository Rule

Every write operation must pass through the Repository.

No exceptions.

---

## Storage Rule

Storage only persists validated Project state.

Storage performs no business validation.

---

## Discovery Rule

Knowledge Discovery is read-only.

Discovery never changes Project data.

---

## Creation Rule

Knowledge Creation requests modifications through the Repository.

It never modifies Project Models directly.

---

## Validation Rule

Validation always occurs before persistence.

---

## Transaction Rule

Every write operation belongs to exactly one Transaction.

---

## Identity Rule

UUIDs remain immutable.

Objects never change identity.

---

## Offline Rule

All Version 1 functionality must work without internet connectivity.

---

# 2.5 Dependency Rules

Dependencies flow downward.

Example:

```text
UI

↓

Workspace

↓

Repository

↓

Project Models

↓

Storage
```

Never reverse this direction.

---

Forbidden:

```text
Storage

↓

Workspace
```

or

```text
Node

↓

UI
```

---

# 2.6 Package Isolation

Every package owns exactly one responsibility.

Examples:

Repository

Coordinates.

Storage

Persists.

Workspace

Presentation state.

Validation

Integrity.

Discovery

Queries.

Creation

Construction.

Packages must not absorb responsibilities belonging to other packages.

---

# 2.7 Forbidden Practices

Implementation must never:

❌ Bypass Repository

❌ Duplicate Project ownership

❌ Duplicate UUID generation

❌ Modify Storage directly

❌ Skip Validation

❌ Ignore Transactions

❌ Create circular dependencies

❌ Hardcode relationships

❌ Mix UI with business logic

---

# 2.8 Code Quality

Implementation should favor:

Small functions.

Single Responsibility Principle.

Composition over inheritance.

Dependency injection where appropriate.

Clear interfaces.

Explicit naming.

Predictable behavior.

---

# 2.9 Performance Goals

Version 1 targets:

Project load:

<2 seconds

Search:

<150 ms

Open Node:

<50 ms

Create Card:

<100 ms

Save Project:

<500 ms

These are goals rather than strict guarantees.

---

# 2.10 Testing Requirements

Every subsystem must include:

Unit Tests

↓

Integration Tests

↓

Acceptance Tests

↓

Regression Tests

Every architectural rule should be testable.

---

# 2.11 Documentation Requirements

Every public interface must be documented.

Every exported type must include descriptive documentation.

Architectural decisions requiring deviation must be recorded in an ADR before implementation.

---

# 2.12 Claude Operating Rules

During implementation Claude should:

✔ Follow architecture.

✔ Explain assumptions.

✔ Suggest improvements separately.

✔ Keep commits modular.

✔ Generate maintainable code.

Claude should not:

✖ Invent features.

✖ Remove existing architecture.

✖ Replace Project Models.

✖ Introduce hidden state.

✖ Ignore specifications.

---

# 2.13 Acceptance Criteria

Implementation constraints are considered satisfied when:

- Repository remains the single write gateway.
- Architectural layers remain separated.
- Dependencies remain acyclic.
- Validation always precedes persistence.
- Tests cover architectural guarantees.

---

# My thoughts after Chapter 2

This chapter is, in my opinion, what separates an implementation guide from an architectural handoff.

Without it, Claude is free to interpret the architecture creatively.

With it, Claude has a clear understanding of **where it has freedom** (code quality, organization, optimization) and **where it does not** (core architectural principles).

---

# Where we go next

Now we move from **rules** to **engineering details**.

The next chapter should be:

## **Chapter 3: Technology Stack & Toolchain**

This is where we lock down:

- Programming language
- UI framework
- Storage technology
- Build system
- Testing framework
- Folder structure
- External libraries
- Dependency policy

This is the last major decision before implementation begins, and once it's written, Claude will know not only **what** to build and **how** to build it, but also **what tools** it must use to build it consistently. I think that makes it the natural next step before we start defining concrete module interfaces.

# MTDP-001
## Chapter 3
# Technology Stack & Toolchain

---

## 3.1 Purpose

This chapter defines the approved technologies, development environment, libraries, and tooling for LoreCanvas Version 1.

The goal is to provide a consistent development experience and avoid unnecessary architectural drift caused by changing technologies during implementation.

---

# 3.2 Platform Targets

Version 1 officially targets:

### Primary Platform

- Windows Desktop (Windows 10 & Windows 11)

### Future Platforms

- Linux
- macOS

The architecture should remain portable even if only Windows is supported initially.

---

# 3.3 Programming Language

**TypeScript**

Reason:

- Strong typing
- Excellent tooling
- Large ecosystem
- Easy maintenance
- Good AI-assisted development support

---

# 3.4 Desktop Framework

**Electron**

Reason:

- Mature ecosystem
- Cross-platform support
- Strong TypeScript integration

Alternative frameworks (such as Tauri) may be evaluated in a future major version, but Version 1 should remain consistent with the selected framework unless there is a compelling reason to change.

---

# 3.5 Frontend Framework

**React**

Responsibilities:

- User interface
- Views
- Components
- Interaction handling

React should not contain business logic.

---

# 3.6 Styling

Recommended:

- CSS Modules

or

- Tailwind CSS

Choose one and use it consistently across the project.

---

# 3.7 State Management

State should be divided into:

### UI State

Examples:

- Sidebar open
- Selected Node
- Active tab
- Window layout

### Project State

Managed through:

Repository

↓

Project Models

UI components should never directly own Project data.

---

# 3.8 Storage

Version 1 should store Projects as structured files.

Example:

```text
Project/
    project.json
    nodes/
    cards/
    links/
    assets/
```

No database is required for Version 1.

---

# 3.9 Testing Framework

Recommended:

- Vitest (or Jest if preferred)

Testing categories:

- Unit
- Integration
- Acceptance
- Regression

Every Repository operation should be testable.

---

# 3.10 Build Tool

Recommended:

- Vite

Responsibilities:

- Development server
- Build pipeline
- Asset bundling
- Hot reload

---

# 3.11 Package Manager

Recommended:

- pnpm

Alternatives:

- npm
- yarn

The chosen package manager should remain consistent throughout the project.

---

# 3.12 Code Quality Tools

Recommended:

- ESLint
- Prettier

These tools should be configured before significant development begins.

---

# 3.13 Version Control

Git is required.

Suggested branching strategy:

```text
main

↓

develop

↓

feature/*
```

Every completed feature should be merged through review.

---

# 3.14 Dependency Policy

External libraries should be added only when they provide clear value.

Preference order:

1. Built-in platform capabilities
2. Small, well-maintained libraries
3. Large frameworks only when justified

Avoid unnecessary dependencies.

---

# 3.15 Logging

Implement structured logging.

Levels:

- Debug
- Info
- Warning
- Error

Logs should assist development without exposing sensitive user data.

---

# 3.16 Configuration

Configuration should be centralized.

Avoid scattered constants.

Examples include:

- File locations
- Limits
- Feature flags
- Debug settings

---

# 3.17 Acceptance Criteria

The technology stack is considered established when:

- All developers use the same core toolchain.
- The project builds consistently.
- Dependencies remain manageable.
- Development tooling is reproducible.

---

## One thing I would change from our earlier discussions

As we've refined LoreCanvas, I think we should treat it as a **modular monolith** for Version 1.

That means:

- One application.
- One process.
- Clearly separated internal modules.

Instead of trying to build lots of independent services from day one.

For an offline desktop application, this keeps development simpler while still preserving the architectural boundaries we've defined. If, years from now, parts of the application need to become separate services, the modular architecture will make that transition much easier.

---

## Before we lock this in

There is one technology choice I'd like us to make together rather than assume:

**Desktop framework: Electron or Tauri?**

Both can support the architecture we've designed, but they have different trade-offs.

- **Electron** has a larger ecosystem, more tutorials, and tends to be easier for beginners. It also aligns well with TypeScript, React, and AI coding tools like Claude.
- **Tauri** generally produces smaller, more memory-efficient applications, but introduces a Rust backend, which adds complexity.

Given that you're learning as you build, using VS Code, and planning to rely on Claude for implementation, I would lean toward **Electron** for Version 1 because it reduces the number of technologies you need to understand while still providing a solid path to a polished desktop application.

If we choose Electron, then I think the technology stack is effectively locked, and the next chapter can begin defining the actual package structure and module interfaces that Claude will implement.

# 🚧 Chapter 4
# Repository & Folder Structure

**Target Length:** 10-15 pages

---

## Chapter Purpose

This chapter defines the physical structure of the LoreCanvas codebase.

Its objectives are:

- Keep the codebase understandable.
- Prevent architectural drift.
- Clearly define ownership of every module.
- Establish dependency boundaries.
- Enable scalable development.

No source file should exist outside this structure unless explicitly approved.

---

# 4.1 Repository Philosophy

The repository is organized by **responsibility**, not by feature.

Each package owns exactly one concern.

This minimizes coupling and keeps the architecture aligned with LAR-001.

The repository is designed as a **modular monolith**.

Modules communicate through well-defined interfaces while remaining part of a single application.

---

# 4.2 Repository Layout

```text
LoreCanvas/
│
├── apps/
│   └── desktop/
│
├── packages/
│   ├── core/
│   ├── repository/
│   ├── creation/
│   ├── discovery/
│   ├── validation/
│   ├── transactions/
│   ├── storage/
│   ├── workspace/
│   ├── ui/
│   ├── common/
│   └── testing/
│
├── assets/
│
├── docs/
│
├── examples/
│
├── scripts/
│
├── tools/
│
├── tests/
│
└── package.json
```

Every directory has a single purpose.

---

# 4.3 Applications

The **apps/** directory contains runnable applications.

Version 1 contains only:

```text
apps/
    desktop/
```

Future versions may introduce:

- Mobile
- Web Viewer
- Companion Apps

without affecting the core architecture.

---

# 4.4 Package Philosophy

Packages are independent architectural modules.

A package may expose a public interface but should hide its internal implementation.

Packages communicate only through documented APIs.

Direct internal access is prohibited.

---

# 4.5 Package Responsibilities

## core/

Contains:

- Project
- Node
- Card
- Link
- Shared domain models
- Domain rules

No UI code.

No storage logic.

No business workflow.

---

## repository/

Responsible for:

- Coordinating writes
- Coordinating reads
- Transactions
- Lifecycle management

Acts as the central gateway.

---

## creation/

Responsible for:

- Creating objects
- Templates
- Wizards
- Default values

Cannot directly modify storage.

---

## discovery/

Responsible for:

- Search
- Filters
- Queries
- Graph traversal
- Timeline generation

Read-only.

---

## validation/

Responsible for:

- Rule checking
- Integrity validation
- Relationship validation
- Project consistency

No persistence.

---

## transactions/

Responsible for:

- Undo
- Redo
- Rollback
- Atomic operations

---

## storage/

Responsible for:

- Reading files
- Writing files
- Version migration
- Backup management

No business rules.

---

## workspace/

Responsible for:

- Active project
- Open panels
- Selection state
- Session information

Does not own Project data.

---

## ui/

Contains:

- React components
- Windows
- Dialogs
- Menus
- Themes

No domain logic.

---

## common/

Shared utilities.

Examples:

- UUID generation
- Logging
- Configuration
- Constants

Must remain generic.

---

## testing/

Contains:

- Shared test helpers
- Mock data
- Fixtures
- Benchmark tools

---

# 4.6 Dependency Rules

Allowed dependency flow:

```text
UI
↓

Workspace
↓

Repository
↓

Core

↓

Storage
```

Validation may be used by Repository.

Discovery may read Core.

Creation may request Repository operations.

---

Forbidden:

- UI → Storage
- Storage → UI
- Core → React
- Core → Electron
- Storage → Repository
- Validation → UI

These are architectural violations.

---

# 4.7 Import Policy

Packages should expose a single public entry point.

Example:

```text
packages/repository/index.ts
```

Internal implementation files must not be imported by other packages.

This keeps refactoring safe.

---

# 4.8 Naming Conventions

Packages:

- lowercase

Folders:

- lowercase

Classes:

- PascalCase

Interfaces:

- PascalCase

Functions:

- camelCase

Constants:

- UPPER_SNAKE_CASE (for true constants) or camelCase for module-scoped immutable values, depending on project convention.

Files:

- kebab-case

Maintain consistency across the project.

---

# 4.9 Ownership

Every source file has one owning package.

No file belongs to multiple packages.

Shared functionality should move into **common/** rather than being duplicated.

---

# 4.10 Acceptance Criteria

This chapter is complete when:

- Every file belongs to one package.
- Every package has one responsibility.
- Dependency flow remains valid.
- Circular dependencies are impossible.
- Package ownership is clearly defined.

---

# MTDP-001
# Chapter 6
# Domain Model Specification

**Target Length:** 10–15 pages

---

# 6.1 Purpose

This chapter defines every domain object used by LoreCanvas.

A domain object is an entity that represents persistent knowledge within a project.

Every domain object must have:

- Clear ownership
- Stable identity
- Defined lifecycle
- Serialization rules
- Validation rules
- Relationship rules

The Repository is responsible for managing these objects.

---

# 6.2 Domain Hierarchy

```text
Project
│
├── Nodes
│     ├── Cards
│     └── Metadata
│
├── Links
│
├── Timelines
│
├── Templates
│
└── Workspace References
```

Everything belongs to one Project.

Nothing exists outside a Project.

---

# 6.3 Domain Rules

Every domain object must:

✔ Have a UUID.

✔ Be serializable.

✔ Be versioned.

✔ Support validation.

✔ Be transaction-safe.

✔ Be exportable.

✔ Be recoverable.

---

# 6.4 Project

## Mission

Project is the root container.

Everything belongs to exactly one Project.

---

### Owns

Nodes

Links

Templates

Timelines

Assets

Metadata

Project Settings

History

---

### Identity

Immutable UUID.

Never changes.

---

### Lifetime

Created

↓

Opened

↓

Modified

↓

Saved

↓

Closed

↓

Archived

---

### Responsibilities

Maintain ownership.

Coordinate persistence.

Provide root lookup.

---

### Never

Contain UI state.

---

# 6.5 Node

## Mission

A Node represents a single knowledge entity.

Examples:

Character

Location

Kingdom

Faction

Magic System

Item

Creature

Event

Religion

Technology

Organization

Concept

### Identity

Immutable.

---

### Owns

Metadata

Tags

Relationships (references only)

---

### Node Lifecycle

Created

↓

Edited

↓

Linked

↓

Archived

↓

Deleted

---

### Constraints

A Node cannot exist outside a Project.

A Node owns its Cards.

Deleting a Node follows the project deletion policy, including validation and cleanup of dependent references according to the rules defined elsewhere in the specification.

---

# 6.6 Card

## Mission

Cards contain information.

They are the primary content units.

---

### Examples

Description

Biography

Statistics

History

Notes

References

Timeline Entries

Documents

---

---

### Ownership

Never multiple.

---

### Lifecycle

↓

Edited

↓

Versioned

↓

Archived

↓

Deleted

---

### Rules

Cards never exist independently.

---

# 6.7 Link

## Mission

### Connects

↓

Node

or

Node

↓

Card

(if supported by the approved model)

Direction

A Link may contain one or more Context objects.

It becomes its own structured narrative.

### Context Objects

# 6.9 Timeline

Timeline is its own first-class model.

Templates never contain Project data.

# 6.12 Domain Ownership Matrix

| Object | Owner |
|---------|-------|
| Project | Repository |
| Node | Project |
| Card | Node |
| Link | Project |
| Timeline | Project |
| Timeline Event | Timeline |
| Template | Project |
| Metadata | Parent Object |

Ownership is singular.

Shared ownership is prohibited.

---

# 6.13 Serialization Rules

Every object must:

Support JSON serialization.

Maintain UUID stability.

Preserve relationships.

Support version migration.

Ignore UI state.

---

# 6.14 Validation Rules

Every object validates:

Identity

↓

Ownership

↓

References

↓

Constraints

↓

Serialization

Validation failures should produce structured errors rather than partial writes.

This chapter is complete when:

- Every domain object has a defined owner.
